extracted.intended_audience: archaeologists submitting preprints and researchers/reviewers/recommenders participating in PCI Archaeology (preprint peer review)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative criteria and expectations used by PCI Archaeology recommenders and reviewers when assessing archaeology preprints (including digital archaeology, methods papers, case studies and tools). Useful for authors preparing preprints and reviewers/recommenders who must evaluate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and reproducible workflows
rubrics_metrics.description: Workflows, tools and analyses should enable reproducibility (e.g., "fully reproducible and accessible data labelling and model training"; replication reports testing reproducibility of bibliometric studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should supply workflows, code and data or clear instructions enabling others to reproduce results; recommenders value frameworks that 'enable fully reproducible' processing and papers that demonstrate reproducibility or explicitly replicate previous studies. Notes in examples: use of open datasets (OpenAlex vs WoS) and archiving on Zenodo support reproducibility; highlight any data-curation limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, transparent description and justification of methods, design choices and processing steps (e.g., 'methodological transparency', 'clear justification for their design choices').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed methods, processing workflows, and rationale for choices (including limitations). Transparency includes archiving developer responses to peer review, describing preprocessing steps, parameter choices, and test procedures so referees and readers can assess validity and reproduce or adapt the approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / contribution to the field
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission should make a meaningful contribution or fill a genuine need in archaeological research or practice (e.g., 'significant contribution to GIS-based analysis', 'identifies a genuine need').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the work matters: what gap it fills, what problems it solves, and who benefits. Recommenders praise contributions that can 'benefit a broad community' or 'establish a standardised protocol' and that enable new lines of enquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence between methods and archaeological reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological design must be coherently tied to the archaeological question or interpretive goal (e.g., 'methodology tied directly to archaeological reasoning', 'coherence of this design').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how each methodological component addresses a specific interpretive question; avoid methods-for-the-sake-of-methods. Papers are stronger when geology, modelling, or digital workflows are explicitly leveraged to test archaeological hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsiveness to peer review and iterative revision
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should engage constructively with reviewers' comments and revise accordingly (e.g., referees suggested improvements which have been addressed; 'iterative responsiveness to peer feedback').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document edits and provide reasoned responses to reviewer concerns. Recommenders value revised versions that improve clarity, address technical faults, or justify retained design choices transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open access, archiving and availability of materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for open-access publication and for archiving code/data/supplementary files (e.g., Zenodo archiving; publication in Peer Community Journal, open-access and free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make datasets, code, models, and developer response documents openly available (preferably with persistent identifiers). This supports reuse, replicability, and community uptake; highlight licences and repository locations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of presentation, figures and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear presentation of results, informative figures, and readable documentation that make workflows and evidence easy to follow (e.g., 'figures are more informative; the workflow and reconstruction are easier for readers to follow').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure figures, captions, and methods sections are comprehensive and clear; present radiocarbon and stratigraphic evidence, workflow diagrams, and stepwise explanations so non-specialist readers can follow the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive restraint and epistemic honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overstatement of results; present conclusions proportionally and acknowledge uncertainty or alternative explanations (e.g., 'avoid overstatement', 'epistemic honesty').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame conclusions as supported by the evidence, discuss limitations, and explicitly state where interpretations remain tentative or where further work is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with literature and theoretical grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should engage appropriately and explicitly with relevant theoretical literature (e.g., expanded theoretical discussion; engagement with archaeological implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate the work within existing scholarship, cite and discuss key debates, and explain how the study advances, tests, or challenges theoretical positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usability and user evaluation for digital tools and interfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital tools, serious games, visualisations and interactive applications should be evaluated for usability and pedagogical/research effectiveness (e.g., 'structured user evaluation', user studies, participant observation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include user testing, questionnaires, interviews or other evaluation methods; report sample sizes and findings; document iterative fixes motivated by usability feedback (motion sickness, HUD issues, navigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinarity and integration of complementary methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective integration of multiple disciplines or methods (e.g., 'integrating civil engineering with climate modeling and seismic risk assessment', 'combining geological modelling, 3D reconstruction and thermal simulation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how interdisciplinary elements combine coherently to address the research question; ensure that each domain's methods are applied at appropriate rigor and that cross-disciplinary assumptions are stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and benefit to the broader research community
rubrics_metrics.description: Work should have potential application or benefit beyond a narrow case study (e.g., 'benefit a broad community', 'establishing a standardised protocol', 'transferable framework').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight generalisability, provide tools or guidelines for adoption, and discuss contexts where the approach would be applicable or require adaptation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical robustness and methodological rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses and computational tools should be technically sound and appropriately validated (e.g., reduced computational intensity, use of FEM, CFD, or validated image-matching pipelines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide validation tests, benchmarks, sensitivity analyses, and comparisons to alternative algorithms; explicitly report limitations (e.g., rotation sensitivity, single-class segmentation limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data interoperability, FAIR principles and choice of ecosystem
rubrics_metrics.description: Digital workflows should prioritise interoperability, openness and alignment with FAIR principles (e.g., QField integration with QGIS/PostGIS, discussion of iDig/ODK limitations vs open GIS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer open formats and workflows that maximise long-term reuse and integration; explain trade-offs between closed specialised systems and open GIS-based environments, including resource/skill requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of framing (research tool vs outreach/product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about the epistemic framing of digital products (e.g., treating a game engine as a research tool vs gamification for outreach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether the work aims primarily at hypothesis generation, research experimentation, outreach, or education; avoid conflating terms (e.g., don't use 'gamification' if no game-design mechanics are employed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical, representational and inclusivity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Address ethical and representational choices in visualisations and reconstructions (e.g., critiques of 'uniform, all-white figure models' and their interpretive/political implications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss choices about human representation, diversity, consent where appropriate, and the interpretive consequences of visual/colour/model choices; acknowledge constraints and plan for improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability and generalisability of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should make clear how methods can be transferred or adapted to other contexts (e.g., 'transferable framework', 'relevant to other territories').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe assumptions and boundary conditions for application elsewhere, provide guidance for adaptation, and supply resources (code, documentation) to facilitate reuse.
